name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Conditions Survey places religious organizations within the broader "Other services" category (NAICS 81), where 11.3% of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, down marginally from 11.6% in the prior period. This figure is the closest available official measure for the sector, though it groups congregations alongside other service businesses rather than isolating them, so it should be read as a rough indicator rather than a precise count of AI-adopting congregations.

On the question of what AI is actually being used for, the picture is sharpest around sermon and worship preparation. Per Notre Dame studies of AI and human formation, a University of Notre Dame professor leading research on AI and religion has argued that using AI to draft anything spoken in worship reflects a basic misunderstanding of what Christians believe is happening when a preacher delivers a homily, pointing to a genuine theological fault line around the practice. The Barna Group, which runs national studies tracking AI adoption and perception among US congregations and ministry leaders, has found that nearly all pastors worry AI could misread scripture, and that most want AI to present every interpretation of a difficult passage rather than settle on a single reading, suggesting clergy are cautious about delegating interpretive authority to automated tools even as adoption spreads.

Gloo, described as the sector's primary tech platform and used by thousands of US churches, positions itself explicitly around values-aligned AI for faith organizations. Its platform includes what it calls a comprehensive evaluation framework measuring AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing, alongside developer tools, knowledge graphs, and specialized agents for ministry workflows. The company frames the core infrastructure problem as siloed congregational data that needs to be unified before organizations can act on it, and it offers API-first support for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, indicating that the more technically sophisticated slice of the sector is moving toward custom-deployed rather than generic consumer AI tools.

The ethics conversation is organized and substantive. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, brings together technologists, scholars, theologians, and clergy specifically to introduce what it describes as humility and historicity into AI development, drawing on the ancient wisdom traditions of the world's religions and noting that 85 percent of the global population claims a religious affiliation, making the ethical stakes broad. The organization connects to the same general concerns that Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good is pursuing through interdisciplinary research and policy work on ethical technology design and deployment. The convergence of these efforts around questions of bias, privacy, human dignity, and the meaning of personhood reflects anxieties that are doctrinal as much as practical.

For an organization deciding whether to deploy, the clearest takeaway is that the sector's own researchers and practitioners draw a firm line between administrative AI use and anything touching pastoral or liturgical functions. Congregation-facing tools for communications, scheduling, or data management face less internal resistance than AI involvement in preaching, scriptural interpretation, or counseling. Gloo's emergence as a sector-specific platform rather than a generic SaaS layer suggests that faith organizations with values-alignment requirements may prefer purpose-built vendors over general-purpose tools, and that the vendor landscape is beginning to reflect this. The Barna Group and Hartford Institute for Religion Research continue to track congregational adoption trends, and their data will likely provide the most usable sector-specific benchmarks as the Census figure remains aggregated across a wide range of service businesses.
